From this period the name of Hijikata Toshizō rises up as a great presence in the history of the Boshin War.

He ran to the Shōnai domain and worked on its lord; he fought in the siege-defense of Aizu-Wakamatsu; and, judging that the course taken by Sendai — the greatest of the great domains of Ōshū — would be the turning-point of the war, he came, to press its decision, into the gaijin-ya (the lodging for guests from outside the domain) at Kokubunchō in the castle-town of Sendai, quartered his two thousand troops in lodgings here and there through the town, and, with armed force for a backdrop, pressed for the settling of the domain's counsels within Aoba Castle.
Autumn comes early in the northeast.
In the temple quarter and the samurai-residence quarter of the Sendai castle-town, the broadleaf trees were already beginning to yellow.

Of Kondō's execution at Itabashi he had, in this interval, heard the full account from an Imperial prisoner during the fighting at Aizu-Wakamatsu, and, choosing a spot on the mid-slope of Atago-yama at Wakamatsu, had raised a gravestone,
Kanten'in-den Jungi Seichū Dai-koji,
and carved on it this posthumous name.
Even after entering the Sendai castle-town, on the twenty-fifth, the death-day, he shunned fish and flesh the whole day through and prayed for the repose of the dead.

Even as he did so, the anti-Satsuma-and-Chōshū volunteers who had broken out of Edo and fought their way across the Kantō gathered in a stream into the Sendai castle-town and looked to Toshizō for command.
Toshizō went up often to Aoba Castle and pleaded his case to the lord, Mutsu-no-kami Yoshikuni, and his retainers.
"Ōshū is one-sixth of Japan,"
was his argument.

"And more: unite the troops of all the Ōshū domains and they come to fifty thousand, hardy in man and horse, better than the men of the western provinces. Hold this country, split the realm in two, then denounce the wrongs of Satsuma and Chōshū, and, if they will not hear, chastise their violence. The martial valor of the Date house has rung through the realm ever since your founding lord, Lord Teizan — Masamune — so I beg you, as head of the Ōshū alliance, to show the whole land where right lies."

Toshizō was pressing his case, as it were, as the representative of the old shogunate. With a vast body of runaway foot-soldiers behind him, this man's every word was enough to shake the Sendai domain.

About this time the Sendai lord, Date Yoshikuni, untied the sword-cord from his own blade and gave it to Toshizō. A sword-cord of pale-blue braided silk, now in the keeping of the Satō house in Hino city.

Meanwhile, on the night of the nineteenth of the eighth month, Enomoto Izumi-no-kami Takeaki, vice-president of the old shogunal navy, led the shogunal fleet out from the offing of Shinagawa in flight and began to steam north.

With the Kaiyō-maru as flagship and the Kaiten-maru, Banryū-maru, and Chiyodagata-maru — four warships in all — accompanied by the transports Shinsoku-maru, Chōgei-maru, Mikaho-maru, and Kanrin-maru, it was the greatest fleet in Japan, and in naval strength the Imperial army came nowhere near it.

This Enomoto fleet carried too the old shogunal soldiers who had broken out of Edo, and aboard as well were the French instructors of the old shogunal army: the artillery officer Brunet, the artillery sergeant Fortant, the infantry sergeants Bouffier and Cazeneuve, and others.
On the way, scattered by wind and wave, it lost two ships, the Mikaho and the Kanrin; but this hardly touched its strength as a fleet.
These gathered, one after another, at Sabusawa harbor and Tōna beach in the Sendai domain, between the twenty-fourth of the eighth month and the eighteenth of the ninth.
The flagship Kaiyō-maru put in on the twenty-sixth of the eighth month, and that same day Enomoto, at the head of his staff and his landing-party, came ashore in full martial array.
Hearing that Hijikata Toshizō and Ōtori Keisuke had set the old shogunal army's headquarters at Kokubunchō, Enomoto decided to hold there, for the present, a conference of the two arms, sea and land.
On the way, Enomoto,
"Arai,"
asked Arai Ikunosuke, the captain of the Kaiyō-maru,
"I know Ōtori well, but what sort of man is this Hijikata Toshizō?"
"I've met him in Edo. A composed, resolute man; in the matter of commanding a great force, perhaps more than Ōtori's equal,"

Arai Ikunosuke, like Enomoto, was of old hatamoto stock, had studied at the shogunate's Nagasaki Naval Training School, and had served as head of the naval drill-yard at Tsukiji Odawara-chō in Edo and as captain of the shogunal ship Juntō-maru — a navy man to the bone, though he had also been an infantry commander for a time.

For his knowledge of meteorology he came, after the Restoration, to a curious second half of life as the first head of the Central Meteorological Observatory. In short, with Enomoto — who had even studied in Holland — at their head, Arai and Ōtori and the like were the very flower of the old shogunate's Western-studies party.
But of the man he was now to meet — Hijikata Toshizō, former vice-commander of the Shinsengumi — he could make nothing. Rather, there was something in it that jarred.

When he reached the lodging at Kokubunchō, Toshizō was out, gone to call on Tomi Kogorō, the Sendai domain's leading advocate of war, who had gathered troops and was quartered at the Dainenji south of the castle.
Asking after Toshizō's repute at the lodging, he found him enormously popular, while of Ōtori no one had much good to say.
A scholar he may be, but a coward — so some flatly declared.
Presently Toshizō came back.
"I am Enomoto Kamajirō,"
said Takeaki.
"Forgive my slowness in naming myself. Hijikata Toshizō,"
— and he smiled, all smiles. For this curt, unfriendly man to break into a broad smile at a first meeting with Enomoto was no small thing.

The Sendai castle-town was in a ferment at the coming of the old shogunal fleet into port. In Kaei 6, the American East India Squadron under Commodore Perry had come and given all Japan a shock; and now a fleet of that same power lay within the domain's waters.

The flagship Kaiyō-maru, for instance, was a newly built Dutch vessel of three thousand tons' displacement and four hundred horsepower; the Kaiten-maru next to her was of 1,687 tons; and the guns of these two ships alone, once they opened fire, would silence the Sendai coastal batteries in an hour.
And she had carried well over a thousand land-troops up from Edo.
"Enomoto, the counsels of the Sendai domain still waver, split between peace and war; but this will avail more than a million words of persuasion,"
"Hijikata, you are the most battle-seasoned man in all the old shogunate. I count on you,"
and Enomoto gripped Toshizō's hand, in the Western manner.
That night a council of war was held, and each man's part was fixed.
From this day Toshizō took the office of rikugun-bugyō-nami, Assistant Commissioner of the Army, with charge over the land forces, and the disposition of the positions was settled.
He set his headquarters on Hiyoriyama.

A low dune to the southwest of the present city of Ishinomaki (on the north shore of Sendai Bay), it was the site of the castle of the Kasai house, the first family of Ōshū in the age of the Northern and Southern Courts.
The hill is low, but commands a wide view of sea and land, and faces Makiyama across the Kitakami River to the east.
Toshizō made his quarters at the Kashima Myōjin shrine at the foot of this Hiyoriyama, and drew up his forces along ten ri of coast, as far as Matsushima and Shiogama.
At this even Enomoto was taken aback.
"Hijikata, surely it would be better to mass the troops in the Sendai castle-town. Why post them out along so long a stretch of coast?"
"No,"
put in Matsudaira Tarō — former infantry commander, now Commissioner of the Army, and well disposed toward Toshizō —
"It is to hold French-style maneuvers and break the spirit of the peace party in Aoba Castle (that is, Sendai Castle). After the maneuvers we bring them at once into the castle-town,"
he said.

In these maneuvers the Western-style infantry unit under Hoshi Juntarō of the Sendai domain took part as well, and a total of over three thousand men, divided into red and white, fought a great mock-battle wholly in the French manner.
The planning of the exercise, of course, its tactics and its combat movements, were directed by the French advisory group.

Toshizō, with Matsudaira and Ōtori, was a supervisor-general of the exercise; and the mark of this man's peculiar quickness of instinct was that in this great maneuver he wholly took in the French method of handling troops.
The artillery instructor Brunet, astonished,
"Hijikata. The emperor of the French would want you for a division commander,"
said, and in all seriousness.

On the third of the ninth month the Sendai domain summoned the chiefs of the old shogunal army to the reception hall within the castle and, together with the domain's representatives, held a council of strategy against the case of an Imperial attack.

But before ten days were out the domain's counsels softened, and on the thirteenth of the ninth month it decided at last to submit to the Imperial army; the war-party's senior men were all at once removed from the domain's key posts.
Enomoto, hearing this news at his lodging in Kokubunchō, was greatly startled,
"Hijikata, come with me,"
and the two went up to the castle together and met Endō Bunshichirō, the executive who had newly taken the reins of the domain.

Endō was of a distinguished Sendai family, holding for generations a fief of 1,800 koku at Kawaguchi in Kurihara district; he had become a domain executive as far back as the first year of Ansei, but, too fierce in temper to suit the domain's chief men, was afterward posted to Kyoto.

In that time he mixed with the loyalist bravoes of the western domains, and on his return preached a violent imperial-loyalist doctrine, for which the pro-shogunate party had him charged with a crime, so that thereafter he had withdrawn to his fief.
The moment the domain leaned toward submission, he was suddenly taken up and reappointed executive.
In the days when Endō was in Kyoto among the bravoes of Satsuma, Chōshū, and Tosa, he had seen the Shinsengumi's power with his own eyes, and hated it.
And that same Hijikata now sat before him.
And what was more, was denouncing the wrongs of Satsuma and Chōshū and pleading for war.
For Endō,
(What is this, this Shinsengumi bandit?)
it was laughable.
Toshizō too, even as he argued, could not shake the feeling that he had seen this new executive's face somewhere before.
(Could it have been in Kyoto, on patrol through the city, that I saw him?)
A man of good memory, once he thought so, the very circumstances of the meeting rose vivid before his eyes.
One winter, coming south down Karasuma-dōri, he had met this man and four or five companions at Shijō-dōri.

In those days, at the sight of a Shinsengumi patrol, even the samurai of a great domain would turn aside down another street, and rōnin and the like would scatter and hide in the alleys; and so it was that time too.
──Hijikata's come.
— so, surely, one of Endō's companions had said. By his topknot, a Tosa rōnin, no doubt.
Judging it a nuisance, they had all scattered.
Only Endō remained. A high retainer of a great domain, he stood haughtily, his hands tucked in his bosom.
Toshizō put him to question.
"Endō Bunshichirō, of the house of Date Mutsu-no-kami,"
the man said.
His hands still tucked in his bosom.
"We question you on official duty. Take your hands from your bosom,"
— and at that Endō laughed through his nose,

"If you would have me take out this hand, take it up with our lord Mutsu-no-kami himself. Unworthy though I am, I am a hereditary retainer of the Date house. I have never taken an order from any but Mutsu-no-kami,"
he said, with a lordly bearing.
──Why, you —
and Nagakura Shinpachi had run his sword half out of the scabbard, but Toshizō stopped him.
"Quite reasonable,"
and, sending all the corpsmen away, he stayed alone and said to Endō,
"It seems I've been offered a quarrel. I'll take it, so draw,"
Five paces between the two of them.
Endō too meant to draw, it seemed: he raised his left hand and loosed the sword in its scabbard-mouth.
Just then, somehow, a midwinter sparrow came fluttering down between the two of them.
(A town sparrow — no fear in it.)
and Toshizō felt, of a sudden, a touch of haiku-feeling. Here came out the habit of Master Hōgyoku, who took his pleasure in bad verse.
Endō stepped forward.
The sparrow flew up with a start.
"Fool — you've scared the sparrow off,"
said Toshizō.
At that instant Endō sprang high and came at him with a drawing-cut straight from the front.
Toshizō dropped his body low. From his right hand the blade traced an arc, clove the air, and struck Endō's sluggish drawing-cut down at the guard.
"Better give up your half-learned swordplay,"
Endō's sword lay on the ground.

"From now on you'd best give up the empty swagger of a man vain of his domain rank, too. It won't pass in the Kyoto of today. We are charged with keeping order in the city. A great man of the Date house ought to understand as much,"
Flinging out the words, Toshizō walked off to the south.
Looking back, those days were, perhaps, his flowering.
And that Toshizō now sat facing Endō, in French-style uniform, as rikugun-bugyō-nami of the runaway shogunal army.
(That Hijikata?)
In Endō's eyes were contempt and hatred.
Enomoto Takeaki pleaded the case.
This was a man who, rare among Japanese, had seen Europe with his own eyes.

He argued from the state of the world, driving home the thesis that Satsuma and Chōshū, holding a boy-emperor as their screen, were seizing power at their pleasure and about to lead the nation of Japan astray.
Toshizō was another matter.
Poor of speech, he had nothing of the world-view of Enomoto's discourse. In the records touching the Sendai side of the Boshin War, Toshizō is set down as having said this:
"For the Sendai domain, whether it is to its profit to submit to the Imperial army or to its profit to fight — that calculation of gain and loss is beside the point,"
was his line.

"To use the younger brother to strike the elder (by the younger brother he means, no doubt, the Three Houses and the collateral houses — Kishū, Bishū, Echizen; by the elder, it seems, the house of Tokugawa), to use the subject (Satsuma and Chōshū) to chastise the lord (the house of Tokugawa): the bonds of human duty are fallen to the ground, the cardinal relations utterly abolished,"
— denouncing the wrongs of Satsuma and Chōshū with the morality of an old order that could not pass in a time of revolution, and,

"There can be no allowing such men to grasp the great government of the realm. Anyone who in the least understands the way of the warrior and knows the teaching of the sages must never side with these Satsuma and Chōshū men. How, then, does your domain see the matter?"

Sad to say, Toshizō was a brawler when all was said, and for pleading a case to the elders of a great domain his discourse was poor stuff — plainly put, not so very different from what a Shimizu no Jirōchō or a Kunisada Chūji might have said.
This man, after all, belonged on the battlefield; such a grand stage did not suit him.

Only, Saitō Hajime and Matsumoto Sutesuke — corpsmen since the Kyoto days, who had gone up to the castle in Toshizō's train and waited in a side room — were quite carried away, and, calling later at the Satō house in Hino, told of the scene:

──Ah, it was a splendid thing. His bearing weighty, the way he set out his case point by point — the very air of a house elder of a great daimyō. We were truly moved by the dignity of manner and presence that came to him so naturally.

So they told it. To the eyes of old comrades like Saitō and Matsumoto, that a scrapping farmer's son from Ishida village in Minamitama district of Bushū, with no schooling but the one sword, should stand and argue the fate of Sendai's 625,000 koku in the great hall of Aoba Castle was, in itself, a marvel.
But it was not Toshizō's scene to play.
Just after, the Sendai executive Endō Bunshichirō said to his colleague Ōeda Magosaburō,
"Enomoto is a man of parts, sure enough,"
— admiring his learning and his political sense; but of Toshizō he passed a savage verdict.
"As for Hijikata, he is a small man of the peck-measure (a little measure, holding but one peck or so) — not worth the discussing,"

Endō was the head of the imperial-loyalist party within the domain, and bore Toshizō a grudge besides; that, no doubt, is why his verdict was so harsh — but it was, more or less, about the truth of it.
After this, back at the lodging, Toshizō said to Matsudaira Tarō,
"A wretched task, that,"
— wiping the sweat away, at his wits' end, and,
"I'm no good in the great hall, after all. A place of raining bullets and a forest of blades is what suits me,"
he said.
Ōtori Keisuke, listening at his side,
"You were up against the wrong man. This Endō I know too. In my student days in Edo he passed for a brilliant scholar even at the Shōheikō,"
he said, as if in cold mockery of Toshizō.
The Shōheikō was, needless to say, the shogunate's official highest seat of learning, the forerunner of today's Tokyo University.
Ōtori, no doubt, meant it as a veiled jab at Toshizō, the unlettered swordsman risen from the peasantry.
Before long the Sendai domain submitted to the Imperial army.
The Enomoto fleet left the Sendai domain and set sail through wind and wave to open a new world in Hokkaidō.
Toshizō is aboard the flagship Kaiyō-maru.
